mechanism: The harness between the model and its tools is modelled as a Petri net: places hold marks for capabilities, approvals and budgets, and a tool call is a transition that fires only if the needed marks exist. An injected request whose marks are missing or already spent is refused whatever its wording. A maximally permissive supervisor allows everything not provably unsafe, and a stricter refinement trades off refusals against the inference cost of an agent that retries after a refusal.
claim: Safe tool execution under prompt injection can be enforced by mark-based supervisory control, with the least-intrusive safe supervisor characterised formally.
why_not_testable: The result is a formal proof; a toy run would test our own code, not the paper's claim.
one_line: A paper treats agent tool calls like a Petri net with spendable tokens, so an injected request is refused because it has no token, not because of its wording.
idea_why: Gating actions on unspent capabilities rather than on prompt content is the same principle the Proteus hook already uses.
breakdown: List each tool action as a transition with its required marks: capability, an approval, a budget count. Keep the marks in a small state file outside the model's reach and check them in a pre-tool hook before the call runs. Decrement budgets on success and refuse when absent. Log refusals so retries after a denial can be counted. The hook in this folder is already a crude version, so the step is to make budgets explicit and per-session.

mechanism: A bubble map plots a token's largest holders as circles and joins wallets that share a funding source or have transferred between each other, so one actor holding supply through many wallets shows as a cluster. Data comes from on-chain token accounts and transfer history. It misses wallets funded separately from exchanges, liquidity pulls, mint authority and honeypot code, which is why clean clusters do not mean safe. Launchers use bundling to fake distribution, and the clustering is how platforms and checkers catch it.
claim: Linked-wallet clustering on a bubble map shows whether a coin's supply is concentrated, sold as a way to avoid rugs.

one_line: Wallet clustering exposes supply held through many linked wallets, but separately funded wallets and LP pulls slip past it.
idea_why: Holder concentration is easy to measure; whether it predicts rugs needs the Grinder's own outcomes to say.
breakdown: Take ten tokens from the Grinder's existing feed and call the public Solana RPC for the largest token accounts of each, then compute the top-ten share. For the top holders, read recent transfer history to see whether two or more were funded by the same wallet. Join the result to what the Grinder already recorded about each token's later outcome to see whether concentration or linkage separates the losers. This is detection for the paper desk only.
